Death With Dignity

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Who life is this? Mine or the states?

Summary:
Dignity SA is a Non Governmental Organisation that petitions for the rights of those that are terminally ill and are wishing to end their own lives on that basis. Avron Moss was one of their most fervent supporters, who recently ended his own life by illegal means. He made sure that he went out with a bang by preparing his funeral to be a memorial to the cause, as well as to his own life. The insert will use the story of the life and death of Avron Moss to consider the legal, political, religious and emotional themes that surround the issue. Euthanasia is an extremely pertinent issue

Dignity SA is willing to give Carte Blanche access to all the footage that they own. There is an array of material, including an interview with Desmond Tutu. Avron’s family will also give the programme access to all the footage that was filmed on Avron’s deathbed and at the funeral.


Further information:
We will also place this in Worldwide perspective and may include film footage an american woman who gripped her nation with the story of her life and decision to end her own life.

INTERVIEW SUBJECTS:

Reubon Moss – Father of Avron Moss
Kevin Moss – Brother of Avron Moss
Representative of Dignity SA: Professor Sean Davison
He was tried for the attempted murder of his terminally ill 85-year-old mother in Australia. He is the spokesperson for the organisation.
Professor Richard Calland – Constitutional Law Professor
University of Cape Town.
Ingrid Anderson – Religious
Pam – Voice Hidden – Tragic Story – Had to help her husband with failed suicide attempt.
Life Insurance Company
Religious Representatives
Emeritus Archbishop Desmond Tutu
John Jeffreys – Deputy Minister of Justice and Constitutional Development - Confirmation required.

Aimee Dollman

Press Release:


Death with Dignity
Should the terminally ill have a legal right to end their own lives? Carte Blanche investigates a poignant and controversial subject debated globally as we encounter people confronted with this choice – like the Capetonian neuropsychologist who fought for his right to die with dignity.


Script:


Avron Moss was the first Pediatric Neuropsychologist in Cape Town, described by family and friends and as an intellectual and a philosopher. He had strong views on the controversial subject of assisted dying.

Avron Moss: You must die dignified. Just go to sleep. Say goodbye to everyone. Go to sleep.

Social media has allowed more and more people to share their stories with a global audience. Like 29-year-old American Brittany Maynard who made a worldwide impact by sharing her decision to end her own life.

Brittany Maynard: I cant even tell you the amount of relief that it provides me to know that I don't have to die the way that it has been described to me. That my tumor would take me on its own.

LINK: The right to life is probably the most important of all human rights but what if somebody's life is made so unbearable through illness that all they want to do is die?

When Avron was diagnosed with terminal cancer in 2014, his brother Kevin was by his side.

Kevin Moss: His oncologist met him whilst he was in hospital in Cape Town and frankly speaking told him he had between 2 and 8 months to live.

Avron knew immediately that he wanted to take control of his own death.

Kevin Moss: He said under so circumstances is he going to sit in a hospital bed riddled with cancer should that day come. He didn't want to go through pain. He was very clear about that.

The practice is legal in the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Switzerland. In a groundbreaking judgment this month, Canada's Supreme Court ruled in favor of Assisted Dying. Brittany was forced to move to Oregon, the first of only five states in the USA to legalize it.

Brittany Maynard: My goal of course is to influence this policy for positive change and I would like to see all Americans have access to the same health care rights.

LINK: There is a strong belief that proper pain management makes the need to legalize assisted dying unnecessary but while everybody has a right to good palliative care does it necessarily contradict the need for legislation?

The hospice movement believes that assisted dying compromises an important chapter of human life.

Liz Gwyther: I think that a lot of the argument for physician-assisted suicide comes from a position of being fearful and imagining the worst about how our end will be. The pain, the distress, the suffering, the burden of care on our families.

Good palliative care strives to bring comfort and emotional well being in the final stages of life. Here, a hospice worker makes a home visit to alleviate the suffering of a terminally ill patient.

Liz Gwyther: What I have experienced with each family that I have been assisting and each family and patient who has been through that journey is that life is very precious to them, that we can control their symptoms, that we can give them good quality of life.

Good hospice care is vital according to Cape Town professor Sean Davison, but a tragic personal experience in New Zealand strengthened his opinion about assisted dying. He was drawn to the cause when his cancer stricken mother resorted to a hunger strike to end her own life.

Sean Davison: And at that stage she begged for assistance to die.

Sean administered a lethal dose.

Sean Davison: The moment she received that morphine, was a moment of celebration. We both celebrated.

Sean was charged with Attempted murder. He took a plea bargain and accepted a conviction of assisted suicide.

Upon his return to South Africa, Sean created the NGO ‘Dignity SA’ to petition for the rights of those that want to die.

Sean met Avron in 2012 when he joined dignity SA – even before his fatal diagnosis.

Sean Davison: He was prepared to be our first applicant to the high court to obtain the right to die legally, with dignity.

Assisted dying is illegal in South Africa, so Legal proceedings began for a high court ruling and with time running out, Avron set about to enjoy the remainder of his life.

Kevin Moss: He managed to have the unique ability to change what is negative, into thinking that it's, there’s a positive. Including his death.

Aimee Dolman was completing her PHD under Avron’s guidance at his renowned Neuropsychology Practice.

Aimee Dollman: But he was just amazing. His attitude, its actually indescribable.

Avron closed down the practice, but they had formed a strong friendship - and Aimee took on the new role of helping him to plan the end of his life – and to tick lifelong dreams off of his bucket list. Avron bought himself a Maserati, and a horse. Aimee shared his passion for horse riding and together they planned a horseshow that he would sponsor and take part in on his horse Gold Dollar.

Aimee Dollman: It was a very emotional moment to watch. I mean most of the people at the show didn’t actually realise that this would be his last competition but you know I knew it would be.

Avron Moss Sound Up: But I did it. There’s a tick off my bucket list and I'm very happy for that.

Avron’s health was drastically deteriorating.

Aimee Dollman: When I saw him that day on the Friday, I said Avron you sounded actually really panicked today and he said I am, I know I don’t have a lot of time left and I didn't realise it would be this quick.

It was becoming clear that he and Dignity SA would never get their day in Court; their only recourse since a draft bill proposing assisted suicide has been gathering dust in parliament since 1998.

Aaron Motsoaledi: You must be aware that governments around the world put up legislation and programs depending in what is the most immediate priority.

That’s Minister Aaron Motsoaledi giving his personal views as to why assisted dying has not yet been debated in Parliament.

Aaron Motsoaledi: It involves quite a lot of professionalism and frankly speaking I don't think politicians have got that type of professionalism. They will approach it with prejudice.

And that is why Professor Landman believes that this will eventually be a decision for the Constitutional Court.

Willem Landman: IT has to do so without fear or favor. If it was simply a matter of public opinion then there would be no role to play for the constitutional court. In any matter not just in this one.

For example Capital punishment, polygamy and abortion

Willem Landman: And I think common law in respect of assisted dying needs to be brought in line with the constitution.

On the 3rd January friends and family gathered with Avron for a photo shoot, unaware that he had ordered illegal medication from Mexico, and planned his own death for the next day.

Sean Davison: He was uncomfortable that it might not work; it could have been a fraudulent product. He even asked me as a scientist to test it.

Without professional help, attempted suicides can often go wrong, leaving patients worse off than before.

Sean Davison: Statistics show that 1 in 4 suicide attempts of terminally ill or elderly people succeed. The others fail.

Avron had recorded a message, which he hoped will one day be played in a courtroom.

Avron Moss: Why would the law wish me to endure the full extent of those lesions and the devastation that they will bring rather than allowing me to die with dignity.

On 4th January 2015, Kevin sat by his brother’s side and held Avron’s hand as he drank the lethal dose.

Kevin Moss: And he said Kev, and this was his final words. He said Kev this is a wonderful thing. I only wish everyone with a terminal illness could experience this...and then his eyes closed and he breathed for another 10 minutes approximately and then his heart stopped.

Aimee, who has since inherited Avron’s beloved horse, Gold Dollar, wasn't there at the end because she believes that he wanted to protect her.

Aimee Dollman: He probably knew that I would be very upset which I was and I might have panicked and I think he knew it would have been very difficult for me.

She did speak at a moving memorial service for him, as did Sean Davison.

Sean Davison (Sound Up): It's a fact that some people will have family member who request assistance to die.

Avron designed his funeral to be a celebration of his life, as well as a testament to the cause.

His wish echoed the view of Brittany Maynard, who took her own life on 01 November 2014. Her mother has continued to fight for the cause since her death.

Brittany Maynard’s Mother: IT's hard to understand until it's in your life and it’s in your world how important this choice to die on your own terms becomes.

Avron understood that many would disagree with his decision to end his life (prematurely), but he believed that each South African should be given right to choose.

Avron Moss: And we live in a democracy and for those who are not religious we have as much right as everybody else to make a choice...
